Good morning to everyone. Thank you very much to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Mediterranean, seated in UNOCT, for convening this important discussion during the General Assembly. As we discuss artificial intelligence, digital governance and trust, I would like to bring an enhanced child protection perspective to this conversation, which many of the previous speakers have already brought, and focus on the impact, particularly of children affected by armed conflict. And I want to also highlight the work that has been done together, as the President of PAM mentioned, on this specific topic for the publication of a report. Much has already been said about how digital technologies are transforming the threat landscape. Armed groups, including those designated as terrorists, are increasingly using social media, messaging applications, online platforms, and emerging technologies to spread propaganda and hate speech, exploit grievances, incite violence, and to recruit children. Increasingly, children are among the audiences being targeted. This is not a theoretical concern for children affected by armed conflict. Over recent years, we have observed a growing convergence between online spaces and child protection risks in situations of armed conflict. While recruitment and use of children has traditionally taken place in communities directly affected by conflict, digital technologies are creating entirely new pathways through which armed actors can reach children directly. Today, recruitment does not happen only in villages, schools, camps or communities. Increasingly, it happens online. Through social media feeds, gaming platforms, encrypted messaging applications, and algorithmic amplification, harmful content can reach children wherever they are, often beyond the visibility of parents, caregivers, teachers, or child protection actors. At my office, that of the Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict, We recently conducted consultations with young people from across Africa in cooperation with the African Youth Envoy on digital risks and opportunities. The messages we heard were strikingly consistent from young people across Africa. Young people expressed concern about misinformation, hate speech, cyberbullying, online harassment, and the misuse of digital platforms to glorify armed groups and spread extremist narratives. Many described how armed actors use social media content to romanticize violence, portray fighters as heroes, and create a sense of belonging, identity, and purpose that can be deeply appealing to children that are facing insecurity, exclusion, or lack of opportunity. For conflict-affected children, these vulnerabilities are often compounded. Many have experienced already displacement, disrupted education, family separation, poverty, or trauma. Armed actors understand these vulnerabilities and actively seek to exploit them. Armed actors rarely recruit through ideology alone. They recruit by pretending to offer belonging where there is isolation. status, where there is marginalization, and certainty, where there are fear and instability. This observation is as true online as it is offline. Artificial intelligence risks accelerating these trends. AI can make harmful content easier to produce, easier to personalize, and easier to disseminate at scale. It can amplify emotional manipulation, reinforce existing biases, and target specific audiences with unprecedented precision. This presents significant challenges for governments, international organizations, technology companies, and importantly, parliamentarians. But from our perspective, this is not only a technology challenge. It is fundamentally a child protection challenge. The rights of children must remain central as debates on digital governance and AI continue to evolve. The Convention on the Rights of the Child applies online just as it does apply offline. Children have the right to protection from violence, exploitation, and abuse, regardless of whether those threats originate in physical environments or digital environments. This principle should guide our collective response. Allow me to offer four brief observations. First, child protection considerations should be systematically integrated into AI governance and digital policy frameworks. As governments and legislatures develop regulatory responses to emerging technologies, child rights must not be treated as an afterthought. Safety by design approaches, age-appropriate protections, and child rights impact assessments should form part of responsible digital governance. Second, and many of you have mentioned this, digital literacy must increasingly be understood as a protection tool. The young people we consulted repeatedly emphasized the importance of equipping children, caregivers, educators, and communities with the skills necessary to identify manipulation, misinformation, and recruitment tactics online. Prevention begins with awareness. Third, engagement with the private sector is indispensable. Technology companies play a critical role in shaping online environments. They have the capacity and the responsibility to identify harmful content, strengthen safeguards, and reduce opportunities for exploitation. Effective prevention, therefore, requires meaningful partnership between governments, industry, international organization, civil society, and parliamentarians. Fourth, we need stronger evidence and research. Technology is evolving rapidly, often faster than policy responses. We must invest in understanding how armed actors use emerging technologies, how children are affected, and which prevention approaches work best. This brings me to the role of parliaments. Parliaments have a unique contribution to make in addressing these challenges. Through legislation, they can help establish balanced regulatory frameworks that protect children while safeguarding human rights and fundamental freedoms. Through oversight, parliaments can hold institutions and companies accountable for the effectiveness of policies and safeguards. Through representation, they can help rebuild the trust that many of you have mentioned between citizens and institutions and contribute to inform public discourse in increasingly fragmented information environments. Parliamentary diplomacy also has an important role to play. Online threats do not respect borders. Lessons learned in one region can inform effective responses elsewhere. Exchanges between parliamentarians can support the development of common principles, promote good practices, and strengthen prevention-oriented cooperation across regions. Allow me to conclude with one final reflection. In discussions surrounding terrorism, violent extremism, and emerging technologies, there is often a strong emphasis on security. Security matters, but when children are involved, a protection lens is essential. Our office has consistently advocated that children associated with armed forces or armed groups should primarily be viewed as children and victims of violence. Experience has demonstrated that protection, rehabilitation, and reintegration approaches are not only consistent with children's rights, they are also critical investments in long-term peace and security. As we enter the age of artificial intelligence, we must ensure that technological innovation is matched by protection. If armed actors are adapting their methods to the digital age, then our prevention efforts must evolve as well. And if trust is one of the defining issues of our time, then protecting children, both offline and online, must be at the center of our efforts to build resilient, peaceful, and inclusive societies. Thank you very much.

Dear Excellencies, dear colleagues, thank you for the opportunity to contribute to this timely discussion. I'm speaking today from UNOCT, where I lead our work on the intersection of violent extremism and AI and PCVE under the Global Programme on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism. Through the programme, we support governments, civil society, youth leaders, practitioners, and law enforcement to better understand and address conditions conducive to violent extremism and terrorism. And building on Undersecretary General Zuv's earlier remarks, I would like to focus on a practical question for today, which is how parliaments can help ensure that AI strengthens prevention rather than amplifying the harms and vulnerabilities already present online. As we've heard today, AI is changing how online content can be produced, adapted, and distributed. It can reduce the time, cost, and skills needed to create persuasive content at scale, including across languages and contexts. And there are two pathways that we need to keep distinct. First, as we've heard, is terrorist and violent extremist actors deliberately misusing AI tools to refine their own propaganda, translate content, and create synthetic material or test ways of reaching new audiences. And the second is AI-enabled services. that may create unintended harms, including where chatbots reinforce users' grievances or paranoia, particularly where safeguards are weak. And these are different problems that require different responses. At the same time, within our own work at UNOCT, we've heard from PCV practitioners and have learned how AI can be used for good to meet prevention objectives. Through the Republic of Korea supported AI and PCV project, which we're currently implementing, we've examined how PCV practitioners are already using AI tools and where they see potential and also what support they need to do so responsibly in a way that minimizes risks and harms. Through this AI and PCV project, we've consulted more than 120 practitioners globally across 45 different countries, and they've identified potential uses of AI, such as detecting and analyzing online narratives and how they're produced, developing their own communication materials and making information more accessible. Yet fewer than a quarter of the PCV practitioners that we heard from are using AI in their own work. And among government practitioners, the practitioners, the figure was around one in 10, so significantly lower. We heard from them and there was real interest in terms of using AI in their work, but also uncertainty about data protection. reliability bias, and the absence of clear institutional guidance. And this points to a clear gap. AI tools are advancing rapidly, but the capacity to make informed decisions about their use is not keeping pace, particularly in community facing settings where local context, trust, and human relationships are central to prevention. And this is where the United Nations Office of Counterterrorism's Counterterrorism Center and the Global PCV Program work is focused. We work with governments, with civil society, with youth, with gamers. We've heard a lot about gamers today, so I'm quite excited to be able to say we work directly with gamers and game developers to really take a look at AI and PCE with respect to their work and how to protect human rights and preserve trust within those prevention realities. And we're now applying this approach through a second phase of work, also generously supported by the Republic of Korea, in which we're providing mentorship to three civil society organizations focused on PCVE. We decided first to focus on civil society organizations, mainly because it's a contained structure where we can implement quite rapidly within the scope of the project's limited time. One organization that we're working with is formalizing governance for existing internal AI use, their own shared tools and data safeguards for staff guidance. Another is defining the safeguards needed before introducing AI into their prevention analysis and journalist work. And a third organization that we're working with is exploring an emotional support chatbot for returnees with a focus on safe design, human oversight, and crisis response pathways. Through this process, we've seen that in some cases, Responsible PCV decision would be to redesign an application or postpone it and sometimes choose not to use AI at all. And this is not a failure of innovation, it's how we protect people and preserve public trust. And this is also where we see parliamentarians having a real practical role to help close the gap between high level AI principles and how these tools are actually used in prevention settings. First, parliaments can ask whether existing frameworks on AI, online safety, data protection, and consumer protection adequately addressed the two distinct risks. So the deliberate misuse of AI by terrorists and violent extremist actors and unintended harms arising from AI enabled services. Second, parliaments can ask, I can make those safeguards meaningful through their budget and oversight functions. For instance, by asking whether there's a clear authority responsible for implementation. whether it has the technical expertise and resources to assess compliance, and whether public procurement and funding frameworks require adequate risk assessment, data protection, testing, and human oversight before AI is introduced into sensitive prevention work. And this is to help ensure that public investment in AI is matched by the institutional capacity and accountability required to use it responsibly. Third, we also see parliaments using committee hearings, inquiries and parliamentary exchanges to ensure that policy and oversight are informed by the realities of implementation. That means hearing directly from those closest to the issue, such as PCV practitioners, community leaders and gamers, as these are the individuals who are dealing with the threat on a day-to-day basis first hand. Building on the close collaboration already underway between Pam, CTED and UNOCT and the work of our colleagues on the model legislative provisions on terrorist misuse of AI program, we'd welcome the opportunity to extend this practical agenda with interested member states and parliaments. We really see a focused exchange in terms of bringing legislators together and government representatives as having real value. Through the global program for PCVE, UNOCT could bring the evidence, the tools, and the lessons from our existing AI and PCV project, including a practice guide on AI and PCVE, which we published earlier this year, and the organizational readiness work that we're currently implementing. And as I've mentioned earlier, we've heard gaming and young people being referenced quite a lot already today, and our global program works directly with these beneficiaries, with young content moderators, individuals that are on gaming adjacent platforms, and youth leaders globally, and have facilitated dialogue with these stakeholders and policymakers to develop common solutions for prevention. For us, the aim would be to move beyond principles to share legislative and oversight practice, examine realistic prevention scenarios, and identify the safeguards institutions need before AI is introduced into sensitive PCV work. This is a concrete way to help ensure that AI serves prevention and public trust by grounding decisions in evidence, community experience, and human rights, and strengthening institution capacity to act responsibly and in accordance with international human rights standards.
